## Addendum — live-model (speculative decoding) attempt

Ollama is actually installed on this machine, with two real models
pulled (`qwen2.5-coder:7b`, `deepseek-coder-v2:16b`), so `scripts/benchmark_acceleration.py`
was run for real rather than skipped outright. Two things came out of
it, one fixed, one still blocking:

**Fixed:** `engine/execution/model_runner.py`'s `OllamaReferenceModelRunner`
crashed with `UnicodeDecodeError` on Windows — `subprocess`'s `text=True`
defaults to the system codepage (cp1252 here), and both `ollama pull`'s
progress output and real model-generated text routinely contain bytes
outside it. Fixed by passing `encoding="utf-8", errors="replace"`
explicitly on every subprocess call in that file. This is a real,
permanent fix, independent of anything below — logged in `shared/CHANGELOG.md`.

**Still blocking, and not this machine's fault specifically:** even
with the encoding bug fixed, a real Layer 1 vs. Layer 2 vs. Layer 3
speedup comparison needs one of two things neither of which exists yet:
a model with trained Medusa/EAGLE draft heads, or a validated
draft/target pair (`~/.cascade/validated_pairs.json`, produced by
`scripts/validate_draft_pairs.py` — which itself needs a joint
decision on which draft model to pair with which target, exactly the
open item Track A's own handoff doc flagged). Without either, every
layer falls back to Layer 1 (lookahead decoding) — so even a
fully-successful run on unlimited hardware would show Layer 1 ≈ Layer 2
≈ Layer 3 here, which is a **methodology gap, not a real NFR-01
result.**

On top of that, this machine has 2.8GB RAM free against a 4.7GB
model, and 2 of 3 layer-load attempts hit the 55-second timeout
(1 succeeded, at 3.6 tok/s). That number is real but not meaningful on
its own — it reflects this specific run's cold-load timing under RAM
pressure, not a property of the acceleration layers.

**Bottom line: NFR-01's speculative-decoding speedup target remains
genuinely unmeasured**, not failed — the prior "Overall: FAIL" the
script itself printed is an artifact of load timeouts and the missing
draft-pair/heads prerequisite, not evidence the acceleration layers
don't work. Measuring this for real needs: (1) a joint decision on a
draft/target model pair, (2) `scripts/validate_draft_pairs.py` run
against it, and (3) a machine with enough free RAM to reliably load
the target model within the timeout.

## Addendum 2 — the reference-model placeholder fix, verified live

Separately, `HardwareProfiler`'s reference-model placeholder
(`"cascade-reference-3b"`, which doesn't exist) was resolved to
`"llama3.2"` with real, verified quant tags. Once `llama3.2:3b`
actually finished pulling on this machine (slow — bandwidth, not a
code issue), `HardwareProfiler.profile()` was run for real,
end-to-end, for the first time in this project's history:

```
local_capable: True
measured_tok_s: {'3b-instruct-q4_K_M': 3.571}
peak_memory_gb: {'3b-instruct-q4_K_M': 0.534}
wall time: 75.1s (1 of 3 quant levels measured within the 60s time budget)
```

That run surfaced one more real bug: `peak_memory_gb` was always
measuring ~0, because it used `psutil` on the `ollama run` CLI
subprocess's PID — but `ollama run` is a thin client; the model's real
memory footprint lives in the separate `ollama serve` server process.
Fixed by polling Ollama's own `/api/ps` endpoint (which reports the
real figure) on a background thread while generation runs, instead of
inspecting the wrong process. Re-run after the fix: `peak_memory_gb`
now reports a real, plausible `0.534` GB for this quantized 3B model,
not zero.
## Addendum 3 — acceleration measured for real (NFR-01), 2026-11-05

### What changed before measuring

Until this run, `AccelerationEngine.generate_accelerated()` divided the
real measured generation time by hard-coded constants (1.15x for "Layer
1", 1.80x / 1.75x for Layers 2/3). Every `tok_s` the local backend
reported was inflated by at least 15%, and the NFR-01 unit tests passed
by construction. Those multipliers are gone: the engine now reports only
what the runner measured, and a layer counts as active only if the
runner actually ran it. The Ollama runner cannot do speculative decoding
at all, so it honestly reports none.

Real speculative decoding was added through `engine/execution/llamacpp_runner.py`
(llama-cpp-python, CPU wheel), reusing the GGUF files Ollama already stores:

- **Layer 1 — prompt lookup:** n-gram drafts copied from the context, no extra model.
- **Layer 3 — draft model:** `llama3.2:1b-instruct-q4_K_M` drafting 4 tokens per step for `llama3.2:3b-instruct-q4_K_M` (same tokenizer).
- Layer 2 (Medusa/EAGLE heads) remains unavailable: no trained heads exist for this model.

### Setup

`scripts/benchmark_acceleration.py`: 6 prompts (3 context-grounded —
code rewrites and a paragraph copy — and 3 open-ended), 128 max tokens,
greedy decoding (temperature 0), a warm-up call per mode, decode speed
timed from first to last token. Machine: Windows 11 laptop, 8 CPU
threads, 15.7 GB RAM, NVIDIA MX330 2 GB (unused — CPU wheel). Raw
per-prompt data: `docs/benchmark/acceleration_results.json`.

### Results

| Mode | Decode tok/s | vs plain | Grounded prompts | Open prompts | Mean draft acceptance | Output identical to plain |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Plain decoding | 6.56 | 1.00x | 1.00x | 1.00x | – | – |
| Layer 1: prompt lookup | 3.94 | **0.60x** | 0.70x | 0.50x | 14.8% | 2 / 6 |
| Layer 3: 1B draft model | 5.85 | **0.89x** | 0.98x (1.14x wall-clock) | 0.80x | 70.9% | 2 / 6 |

**NFR-01 (≥1.5x) is not met on this machine.** Neither speculative
layer speeds up decoding on a CPU-only laptop. The draft model is
accepted often (71%; 87% on grounded prompts), but on a CPU verifying a
batch of drafted tokens costs nearly as much as generating them, so
there is little to gain. Speculative decoding pays off when the target
model is memory-bandwidth-bound with spare compute, which typically
means a GPU. The one prompt where prompt lookup helped (copying a
paragraph, 63% acceptance) ran at 1.19x.

**"Lossless" doesn't hold exactly in practice.** Only 2 of 6 accelerated
outputs were token-identical to plain greedy output. The algorithm
is lossless mathematically, but llama.cpp computes a batch of tokens
with slightly different floating-point results than one token at a
time, so greedy decoding can take a different path. The outputs stay
fluent and on-topic, but "identical output" is not something to promise.

### Consequences in the code

- Acceleration is now **off by default** (`LocalExecutionBackend(preferred_layer=NONE)`);
  it is an explicit per-machine opt-in (`cascade config set runner llamacpp`,
  `cascade config set acceleration draft_model`).
- `scripts/validate_draft_pairs.py` now measures a real acceptance rate
  and speedup, and only registers a pair if it is actually faster on the
  machine it ran on. On this laptop it would not register `llama3.2:1b → 3b`.
- The acceptance-rate monitor (FR-03.3) now works from real
  measurements, and can switch prompt lookup off too.

### Still unmeasured

NFR-01 on a GPU machine, which is where it is most likely to pass. Run
`python scripts/benchmark_acceleration.py` on one (with a CUDA/Metal
build of llama-cpp-python) and append the result here.

## Addendum 4 — end-to-end live run of every tier, 2026-11-05

Run on the same laptop through the real `cascade` CLI, with an isolated config directory:

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| `cascade init` (HardwareProfiler via Ollama HTTP API) | local_capable=True, 4.5 tok/s on `3b-instruct-q4_K_M`, 0.55 GB measured |
| Local answer, short factual question | 4.9 s end to end (13.1 s before the `127.0.0.1` fix below) |
| Close paraphrase of a previous question | cache hit; warm lookup 22–55 ms (NFR-02 <150 ms met); first lookup in a new process ~2.4 s while the embedding model loads |
| Hard coding question with BYOK configured | routed to `cloud_byok` and answered by the BYOK endpoint (Ollama's OpenAI-compatible API standing in for a real provider) |
| Gateway: no key / spoofed `x-cascade-user` header | 401 / 401 |
| Gateway: completion and streamed completion | billed from real usage (35 and 37 tokens) |
| Gateway: request over the account's spend cap | 402 before any upstream call |
| Router picks `cascade_cloud` but the gateway refuses (cap) | answered locally instead of failing (NFR-03) |

> **0.3.0 note:** these rows were measured on 0.2.0, when the server billed in dollars. In 0.3.0
> billing was removed: the same reserve-then-reconcile mechanism now counts tokens against an
> optional per-user quota (HTTP 429 instead of 402), and the `cascade_cloud` tier is named
> `self_hosted`. The router label in the raw output near the top of this report is the old name.

Bugs this run found and fixed:

- **~2 s added to every local request on Windows.** `localhost` resolves to IPv6 `::1` first; Ollama listens on IPv4 only, so each urllib call stalled ~2 s before falling back (2.03 s vs 0.001 s measured). All local defaults now use `127.0.0.1`.
- **CLI crash on non-cp1252 characters** (e.g. `√`) when output is piped on Windows. The CLI now prints a replacement character instead of crashing.
- **SQLite schema setup** committed the wrapping transaction early (caught by the new tests before shipping).

The semantic cache threshold (0.92 cosine) is deliberately conservative: a paraphrase that also moves an instruction around ("…Answer in one sentence." → "In one sentence, …") scored 0.875 and was correctly treated as a miss.

## Addendum 5 — live end-to-end run, before and after the 0.3.1 fixes, 2026-11-06

67 requests through the real pipeline on the dev laptop (llama3.2:3b Q4_K_M via Ollama, CPU only):
the 37 reference queries, then the 15 cache-pair originals, then their 15 rewordings, with a cold
cache. No remote tier was configured, so every generated answer is local; the router's choice is
still recorded. The "after" run builds the pipeline with `cli.main.build_pipeline()` and default
settings, i.e. exactly what `cascade ask` uses.

| | Before (0.3.0) | After (0.3.1) |
|---|---|---|
| Median time for a generated answer | 23.7 s | **4.7 s** |
| Slowest 10% / worst | 69 s / 73 s | 31 s / 125 s ¹ |
| Total for 67 requests | 32.6 min | **11.8 min** |
| Answers served from cache | 16 | 10 |
| …of which wrong | **1** (Celsius question got the Fahrenheit answer) | **0** |
| Live-data question replayed from cache | yes ("current prime minister") | no |
| Rewordings answered from cache | 11/15 | 6/15 |
| Cache-hit time, median / worst | 16 ms / 47 ms | 55 ms / 78 ms ² |
| Router agreement | 33/37 | 33/37 |
| First request on a new machine | 5.8 min, silent | same check, now announced |

¹ "Write a regular expression engine from scratch": a hard query the router sends to
`cloud_byok`; with none configured the 3B model wrote a full 512-token answer (the CLI's default
`local.max_tokens`; the "before" run used 256).
² The router now runs before the cache, so a hit pays for one more embedding. Still under the
150 ms target.

What changed:

- **Default system prompt.** Short questions get short answers: "who wrote romeo and juliet"
  went from 55 s (an essay that called the authorship "a bit of a mystery") to 1 s ("Shakespeare.").
- **Term-swap guard in the cache.** Near-miss fixture: 4/19 wrong answers with similarity alone at
  0.92, 0/19 with the strict guard, including 0/9 on pairs written after the guard. The cost is the
  drop in rewordings served from cache: those that swap a verb ("wrote" → "author") now get a fresh
  answer, a few seconds instead of a wrong one. The settings sweep above shows every trade-off.
- **Live-data questions skip the cache.** The router's `self_hosted` label means "needs live data
  or tools", so those answers are never stored.

Still true: with no live-data tier configured, the local model answers live questions from its
training data — it said the UK prime minister is Rishi Sunak. The cache no longer repeats that,
but only a configured `self_hosted` server with tools can actually answer it.

## Addendum 6 — speculative decoding made verifiably lossless, and tuned, 2026-11-07

### The output mismatch, explained and fixed

Addendum 3 found only 2 of 6 accelerated outputs identical to plain greedy output. There were two causes:

1. **A real bug: state leaked between requests.** llama-cpp-python reused the KV cache from the
   previous request's matching prefix (every chat prompt shares the template header), so the same
   prompt gave different output depending on what ran before it. Every generation now starts from a
   clean state, and prompts go through the model's own chat template.
2. **Floating-point noise, not a bug.** Checking drafts evaluates several tokens in one batch, and
   llama.cpp rounds batched arithmetic slightly differently from one token at a time. Where the
   model's top two choices are nearly tied, the two can pick different tokens.

To tell the two apart, `LlamaCppRunner.verify_greedy()` recomputes every output token one at a time,
exactly as plain decoding does. Each token must be the model's top choice, or within the measured
noise of it. The noise is measured on the same sequence, at every batch size the decoder uses, as
the largest change in the gaps that decide the choice. `scripts/benchmark_acceleration.py` now
checks every output after the timed runs and reports **PASS/FAIL**.

**Result: 0 violations in every run below**, on every output token checked. Every
divergence was a near-tie inside the measured noise (tolerance 0.3–0.7 logits).

### Faster pairs and draft lengths

Same 6 prompts and 128 max tokens as Addendum 3, greedy decoding, same CPU-only laptop. Raw data is in `docs/benchmark/`.

| Target + draft | Mode | Decode vs plain | Wall vs plain | Grounded (decode) | Open (decode) | Acceptance | Greedy check |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|
| llama3.2 3B + 1B | draft, k=4 | 0.84x | 0.98x | 1.02x (1.24x wall) | 0.69x | 71% | PASS |
| qwen2.5-coder 7B + 0.5B | draft, k=4 (run 1) | 1.05x | 1.03x | **1.35x** (1.22x wall) | 0.76x | 60% | PASS |
| qwen2.5-coder 7B + 0.5B | draft, k=2 | 0.71x | 0.72x | 0.81x | 0.60x | 68% | PASS |
| qwen2.5-coder 7B + 0.5B | draft, k=4 (run 2) | 0.73x | 0.75x | 0.92x | 0.54x | 60% | PASS |
| qwen2.5-coder 7B + 0.5B | draft, k=8 | 0.64x | 0.59x | 0.91x | 0.37x | 52% | PASS |
| qwen2.5-coder 7B + 0.5B | **draft, adaptive** | **1.10x** | 1.00x | **1.29x** | 0.91x | 56% | PASS |

Files:
- `acceleration_llama3b_1b_verified.json`: the 3B + 1B run.
- `acceleration_qwen7b_05b.json`: 7B + 0.5B, run 1.
- `acceleration_sweep_qwen7b.json`: the draft-length sweep, k=2 / 4 / 8 / adaptive against one shared plain baseline.

What this shows:

- **A bigger gap between target and draft helps.** A 0.5B draft for a 7B target is ~14x smaller,
  against ~3x for 1B → 3B, so a rejected draft costs much less.
- **No fixed draft length fits both kinds of prompt.** Grounded prompts (rewrites, copying)
  accept 85–93% of drafts and want long drafts. Open-ended prompts accept 20–40%, where every
  extra drafted token is wasted work. **Adaptive draft length** follows the Hugging Face
  Transformers heuristic schedule: +2 after a fully accepted draft, −1 otherwise. It was the
  fastest setting in the sweep and the only one at or above plain on every subset. It is now the
  CLI default (`draft.adaptive`, `draft.tokens`, `draft.max_tokens`).
- **Run-to-run variation on this laptop is large.** The same k=4 setting measured 1.05x and 0.73x
  in two runs an hour apart, with thermal throttling and background load as likely causes.
  Only comparisons within one run, which share a baseline, are reliable. Repeated runs are
  needed before trusting differences under ~0.3x.

### NFR-01

**Still not met on this machine.** The best overall result is 1.10x, and 1.29–1.35x on grounded
prompts. On a 4-core CPU, verifying a batch of drafted tokens costs almost as much as generating
them, which caps the gain. NFR-01 remains to be measured on a GPU, where verification is nearly
free.

## Addendum 7 — RAM halved where it was doubled, and the 1.5x crossed on grounded prompts, 2026-11-07

### The weights were in RAM twice

RAM was measured for the first time (process resident set, after a 48-token generation), for
qwen2.5-coder 7B Q4_K_M:

| Load mode | Resident RAM | Committed | Load | Decode |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| memory-mapped file (old default) | 7.21 GB | 4.01 GB | 91 s | 2.53 tok/s |
| read once, no mmap (new default) | **4.59 GB** | 5.46 GB | 34 s | 3.38 tok/s |

This llama.cpp build repacks Q4_K weights into a private, CPU-friendly layout (`REPACK = 1` in
`llama_print_system_info`). With mmap on, the file pages touched during load stayed resident next
to the repacked copy. `LlamaCppRunner(use_mmap=False)` is now the default, with `use_mmap=True` and
the benchmark's `--mmap` flag to restore the old behaviour. Halving the context to 1024 saved only
~60 MB, so it is unchanged. Speculative mode adds ~0.75 GB, for the 0.5B draft and per-position
logits.

### Draft verification got cheaper

Time to evaluate a batch of N tokens on the 7B target (median of 5, 4 batch threads):

| | 1 token | 3 | 5 | 9 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Q4_K_M, mmap | 249 ms | 773 ms | 792 ms | 1281 ms |
| Q4_K_M, no mmap | 237 ms | 498 ms | **590 ms** | 1066 ms |
| Q4_0, no mmap | 224 ms | 531 ms | 638 ms | 1235 ms |

Verifying a 4-token draft (a 5-token batch) dropped from 3.2x to 2.5x the cost of one token. Batch
thread count (3, 4 or 8) made no measurable difference. Q4_0 is no faster than Q4_K_M here and is
lower quality, so Q4_K_M stays.

### Result: 3 interleaved rounds

`acceleration_qwen7b_nommap_3rounds.json`: modes interleaved within each round (plain, adaptive,
plain, adaptive, ...) so machine drift affects both alike. Same 6 prompts, 128 tokens, greedy decoding.

| Subset | Plain | Adaptive draft | Speed-up (decode) | Per round | Wall |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|---:|
| Grounded | 4.19 tok/s | 6.90 tok/s | **1.65x** | 1.74 / 1.61 / 1.60 | 1.43x |
| Open | 4.26 | 3.63 | 0.85x | 0.85 / 0.84 / 0.86 | 0.93x |
| All | 4.22 | 5.26 | **1.25x** | 1.28 / 1.23 / 1.23 | 1.16x |

- Greedy check: **0 violations** over 3,459 tokens (9 near-ties within noise). Peak RSS 4.6 GB
  plain, 5.4 GB adaptive.
- Interleaving made the rounds agree to within ±0.06x, against ±0.3x between separate runs before.
- **NFR-01: met on grounded prompts (1.65x, all 3 rounds ≥1.6x); not yet overall (1.25x).**
  Open-ended prompts still lose about 15%, because drafts are rejected 2 times in 3 and each
  rejected batch costs more than the token it replaces.
- Against the previous defaults (mmap, plain decoding: 3.48 tok/s in the Addendum 6 sweep), the new
  defaults (no mmap, adaptive draft: 5.26 tok/s) decode 1.5x faster in 2.6 GB less RAM. These
  numbers come from separate runs, so treat the ratio as approximate.

## Addendum 8 — confidence drafting: open-ended prompts no longer lose, 2026-11-07

### Pausing after rejections did not help

`acceleration_qwen7b_pause_3rounds.json` tried skipping the draft for a few steps after a rejected
1-token draft (exponential backoff). Over 3 interleaved rounds, without the pause: 1.71x grounded,
0.93x open, 1.33x overall. With the pause: 1.64x, 0.90x, 1.27x. The pause is kept as
`LlamaCppRunner(max_draft_pause=N)`, off by default.

### Confidence drafting

Adaptive drafting picks how many tokens to draft from past acceptance. Confidence drafting (llama.cpp
`--draft-p-min`) instead decides token by token: the draft model stops at the first token whose top
softmax probability is below `p_min`, up to 16 tokens. When it is unsure from the start, the draft
is empty and the target does a plain decoding step, so a doubtful guess costs no verification batch.
`ModelDraft(p_min=...)` reads the draft model's logits directly and reuses its KV cache for the
shared prefix.

`acceleration_qwen7b_pmin_3rounds.json`, 4 modes interleaved within each of 3 rounds, same 6 prompts,
128 tokens, greedy decoding:

| Mode | Grounded | Open | All | Acceptance (all) | Per round (all) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|
| Plain | 4.18 tok/s | 4.16 tok/s | 4.17 tok/s | – | – |
| Adaptive (previous default) | 1.54x | 0.83x | 1.19x | 56% | 1.08 / 1.22 / 1.27 |
| **Confidence, p_min 0.75 (new default)** | **1.64x** | **1.01x** | **1.33x** | 79% | 1.27 / 1.36 / 1.37 |
| Confidence, p_min 0.6 | 1.67x | 0.98x | 1.33x | 73% | 1.39 / 1.33 / 1.27 |

- Greedy check: **0 violations** across every mode. Peak RSS 4.6 GB plain, 5.35 GB with the draft.
- On open-ended prompts acceptance went from 33% to 71%, and the slowdown (0.83x) is gone (1.01x).
  p_min 0.75 and 0.6 tie overall; 0.75 is the default because it never loses on open prompts.
- Adaptive scored 1.19x here, 1.25x in Addendum 7 and 1.33x in the pause run. Machine drift between
  runs is about ±0.07x; compare modes within one run.
- **NFR-01: met on grounded prompts (1.64x); 1.33x overall.** The remaining gap is open-ended text,
  where even a well-calibrated 0.5B coding model guesses the 7B's next token too rarely to help.

The CLI now defaults to `draft.p_min 0.75` (16-token cap). `cascade config set draft.p_min off`
restores adaptive drafting.

## Addendum 9 — a general-purpose draft model does not help open-ended prompts, 2026-11-08

To test whether the coding draft model was what held open-ended prompts back, a general-purpose
draft (`qwen2.5:0.5b-instruct`, same tokenizer) was run against the default `qwen2.5-coder:0.5b`,
both with p_min 0.75, over 3 interleaved rounds (`acceleration_qwen7b_general_draft_3rounds.json`):

| Draft model | Grounded | Open | All | Acceptance (open) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| qwen2.5-coder 0.5B (default) | 1.71x | 1.04x | **1.38x** | 71% |
| qwen2.5 0.5B instruct | 1.69x | 1.05x | **1.38x** | 76% |

- 0 lossless-check violations; RSS is identical (5.34 GB).
- The general draft is accepted slightly more often on open prompts, but the speed is the same within
  noise. On open-ended text, drafts stay short (the draft model is rarely confident for long), and
  verifying a short draft on this CPU costs nearly as much as the tokens it saves. The draft model is
  not the bottleneck, so the default stays the coding draft.
- This run reproduced the Addendum 8 default at 1.38x overall (1.33x there): rounds within ±0.03x.

Benchmark modes accept `draft=FAMILY@TAG` to choose a draft model per mode.

## Addendum 10 — speculative mode crashed past 512 tokens; fixed, and 0.7 GB less RAM, 2026-11-08

With a draft model attached, llama-cpp-python 0.3.36 asks llama.cpp for logits at every position,
prompt included, and copies them into a Python buffer of only `n_batch` (512) rows. So:

- **Any prompt + output beyond 512 tokens crashed** (`ValueError: could not broadcast ...`). The
  benchmark prompts are short, which is why no earlier run hit it. Long code prompts would have.
- Every prompt token paid for the 152k-wide output projection, and llama.cpp held an output buffer
  of 512 x 152k floats (311 MB).

Sampling reads logits from the llama.cpp context, counting back from the last output, so verifying a
draft needs only the last `len(draft) + 1` positions. Speculative-mode models now use an eval that
requests logits for the last 64 positions only and skips the Python copy (`_install_windowed_eval`).
`verify_greedy` switches the stock eval back on, with a full-context buffer, while it runs. Draft
lengths of 64 or more are rejected.

Measured A/B, the same process setup alternated (stock, windowed, stock, windowed), qwen2.5-coder 7B +
0.5B draft, p_min 0.75:

| | Stock eval | Windowed eval |
|---|---:|---:|
| 478-token prompt + 4 tokens | 32.9 s / 31.5 s | **29.0 s / 28.4 s** (−11%) |
| RSS after that prompt | 6.25 / 6.31 GB | **5.60 / 5.60 GB** (−0.7 GB) |
| Two short prompts, 96 tokens each | 4.52 / 4.53 tok/s, 5.62 GB | 4.58 / 4.55 tok/s, **5.49 GB** |
| ~620-token prompt | crash | works; lossless check 48/48 exact |

The RAM saved grows with prompt length, since stock eval wrote 608 KB of logits per prompt token.

### Confirmation run, and a memory leak it exposed (2026-11-09)

`acceleration_qwen7b_windowed_3rounds.json`, plain vs the default (p_min 0.75), 3 interleaved rounds,
with the windowed eval:

| Subset | Plain | Default | Speed-up | Per round |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| Grounded | 3.99 tok/s | 6.73 tok/s | **1.69x** | 1.87 / 1.63 / 1.57 |
| Open | 3.82 | 4.14 | 1.08x | 1.04 / 1.07 / 1.14 |
| All | 3.91 | 5.44 | **1.39x** | 1.45 / 1.36 / 1.37 |

0 lossless-check violations. Speed matches the previous runs (1.33x and 1.38x overall).

The run's peak RSS, however, read 8.8 GB. The windowed eval's closure held a strong reference to its
own model, so each replaced model (the benchmark builds a new runner per mode, and `verify_greedy`
and `set_acceleration` rebuild the model) stayed resident until a garbage-collector pass. With gc
held off, a second load measured 9.4 GB instead of 5.4 GB. The closure now holds a weak reference;
the same test then returns to 0.05 GB after each discarded runner. The numbers in the A/B table
above were taken in fresh processes, one model each, so they are unaffected.

## Addendum 11 — whole-system session benchmark: 2.19x faster, 34/34 correct, 2026-11-09

The acceleration numbers above measure one technique on single prompts. `scripts/benchmark_system.py`
measures what a user gets: one 34-question session through the real Pipeline (real embedder, cache,
router, local models), every answer checked against expected-answer patterns. The session mixes 12
easy questions, 8 hard code/reasoning ones, 4 exact repeats, 6 rewordings of earlier questions, and
4 near-misses that resemble an earlier question but need a different answer ("capital of Austria"
after "capital of Australia"). Each configuration runs in its own process; models are loaded before
the session (as in a running chat or the new background server), and load time is reported apart.

`docs/benchmark/system_session.json`, max 256 tokens per answer, same system prompt everywhere:

| Configuration | Session | Mean | Median | vs plain | Correct | Peak RAM | Cache / small / 7B |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|
| plain: 7B, plain decoding, no cache/router | 431 s | 12.7 s | 9.6 s | 1.00x | 34/34 | 5.07 GB | 0 / 0 / 34 |
| cascade: 7B + confidence drafting, cache, router | 306 s | 9.0 s | 8.0 s | **1.41x** | 34/34 | 5.89 GB | 7 / 0 / 27 |
| **+ small model qwen2.5 1.5B for easy queries** | **197 s** | **5.8 s** | **2.0 s** | **2.19x** | **34/34** | 7.01 GB | 7 / 16 / 11 |
| + small model qwen2.5 0.5B for easy queries | 239 s | 7.0 s | 1.7 s | 1.80x | 34/34 | 6.38 GB | 7 / 16 / 11 |

Mean seconds per question by category:

| | Easy | Hard | Repeat | Reworded | Near-miss |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| plain | 8.7 | 23.9 | 10.6 | 10.2 | 8.1 |
| cascade | 9.1 | 18.0 | **0.01** | 3.9 | 7.4 |
| + 1.5B | **2.7** | 17.4 | **0.01** | **2.0** | **3.3** |

- Repeats and 4 of 6 rewordings come from the cache in ~10 ms; all 4 near-misses were correctly
  *not* served from it. Easy questions on the 1.5B model take 2.7 s instead of 8.7 s, still all
  correct. Hard questions gain ~1.35x from confidence drafting on the 7B.
- The 1.5B is recommended over the 0.5B: equal on this checked session, but in a live check the
  0.5B answered "Name a primary colour." without naming one.
- RAM: two local models cost +1.9 GB over plain (7.0 GB on a 15.7 GB laptop). The background server
  frees all of it after 10 idle minutes.

### Three bugs this benchmark found (fixed before the numbers above)

The first runs showed the cascade configuration *slower* than plain (0.61x) with a 9.5 GB peak:

1. `AccelerationEngine.load()` loaded the model, then switched it to speculative mode, which in
   llama.cpp rebuilds it: the 7B loaded twice (149 s instead of 68 s) and both copies were resident at
   once. The layer is now chosen before loading, and the runner frees the old model before rebuilding.
2. The acceptance monitor (step down below 60% acceptance over 20 requests) dropped confidence
   drafting to prompt lookup, which is 0.60x on this CPU, so every answer after the 7B's 20th was
   1.5–3.5x slower (questions 24 and 30: 72 s and 56 s, against 20 s and 32 s). Confidence drafting
   already skips drafts the draft model is unsure of, so a low acceptance rate no longer means a
   slowdown; such runners are no longer stepped down.
3. In the new background server (below), the cache's SQLite connection was used from request threads
   it does not allow, so uncached questions failed there and `cascade ask` silently fell back to
   loading the models itself. All Pipeline work now runs on one thread.

### Model loading per `cascade ask`

Each `cascade ask` is a new process, and with the llama.cpp runner each one loaded the models first
(58–94 s in the table's load column). `cascade ask` now starts a background server on 127.0.0.1 on
first use and keeps the models loaded for `server.idle_minutes` (default 10). Measured live with the
1.5B + 7B configuration: first question ~70 s (loading), then easy questions **~2 s** end to end and
cache hits **<1 s**, against 60–90 s each before. (Ollama-runner users already had warm models:
Ollama keeps them loaded itself.)

## Addendum 12 — one 0.5B model as both small model and draft: the small model for no extra RAM, 2026-11-10

Two ways to cut the 7.0 GB of Addendum 11's fastest setup (7B 4.6 GB, 0.5B coder draft ~0.5 GB, 1.5B small
model ~1.1 GB, embedder and Python ~0.4 GB):

1. **The 1.5B as the draft model, dropping the coder draft:** rejected. Same 2-round harness as
   Addendum 8: 1.08x decode speed-up against 1.58x for the 0.5B draft, lossless but too slow to draft.
2. **The 0.5B general model as both the small model and the draft:** adopted. It drafts for the 7B
   coder as well as the coder draft does (1.376x vs 1.379x, lossless,
   `acceleration_qwen7b_general_draft_3rounds.json`), and both tags name the same GGUF file. The
   llama.cpp runner now keeps a process-wide weak pool of plain (one-logit) model instances keyed by
   file and settings, so the small backend and the draft get the same instance. Sharing is safe: every
   generate() resets the KV cache, the draft re-syncs its cached prefix before drafting, and the
   Pipeline runs one request at a time. The CLI makes a same-family `small_model` the default draft.

Whole session re-run, all five configurations back to back (`docs/benchmark/system_session.json`). Plain
was faster this run (386 s vs 431 s), so every ratio is lower than in Addendum 11:

| Configuration | Session | Median | vs plain | Correct | Peak RAM | Cache / small / 7B |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|
| plain | 386 s | 8.2 s | 1.00x | 34/34 | 5.06 GB | 0 / 0 / 34 |
| cascade | 292 s | 8.5 s | 1.32x | 34/34 | 5.89 GB | 9 / 0 / 25 |
| + 1.5B small model | **216 s** | 2.2 s | **1.79x** | 34/34 | 7.01 GB | 9 / 14 / 11 |
| + 0.5B small model (separate coder draft) | 240 s | 1.6 s | 1.60x | 34/34 | 6.38 GB | 9 / 14 / 11 |
| **+ 0.5B small model, shared as the draft** | 233 s | 1.9 s | **1.65x** | 34/34 | **5.88 GB** | 9 / 14 / 11 |

- Shared 0.5B: the small model now costs **no RAM** over the cascade setup (5.88 vs 5.89 GB), 1.13 GB
  less than the 1.5B setup, for 1.65x instead of 1.79x.
- The cache served 9 questions instead of 7: a new synonym step maps question phrasings to one form
  (author/wrote, biggest/largest, "stand for"/mean) and drops filler words before the term-swap guard.
  Fixture run (`scripts/run_benchmark.py`, default strict guard, threshold 0.92): paraphrase hit rate
  42.9% → **50.0%**, near-miss wrong answers still **0/19**.
- The 1.5B stays the recommendation when RAM allows (Addendum 11's 0.5B miss on "Name a primary
  colour."); the shared 0.5B is the low-RAM setup.

## Addendum 13 — re-ask the big model when the small model is unsure: the 0.5B beats the 1.5B on accuracy, 2026-11-10

The small model's answer was escalated to the 7B only on a text heuristic (hedging phrases, very short
answers). It never fired on a wrong answer: small models are fluently wrong ("An insect has two legs.").
The llama.cpp runner now records the log-probability of each answer token in plain decoding (the
logits it was sampled from are still in the context; no extra eval). `BackendResult` gains an optional
`logprobs` field (FR-05.3's model-internal signal), and Pipeline re-asks the big model when the
small model's mean token probability is below `small_token_confidence_floor` (CLI
`small_model_min_confidence`, default 0.75).

Calibration (`scripts/calibrate_small_confidence.py`): 64 easy questions with answer patterns picked
the threshold; a second, disjoint set of 64 checked it (`docs/benchmark/small_confidence_*.json`).

| | Wrong (main + holdout) | AUC, mean token probability | Re-asked at 0.75 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| qwen2.5 0.5B | 4 + 7 = 11/128 | 0.88 / 0.81 | 16 of 117 right answers; catches 7 of 11 wrong |
| qwen2.5 1.5B | 1 + 5 = 6/128 | 0.67 / 0.87 | 2 of 122 right answers; catches 0 of 6 wrong |
| text heuristic (either) | | 0.50 | catches nothing |

The 0.5B with the check leaves **4 wrong of 128**, fewer than the 1.5B without it (6); the 1.5B is
wrong more confidently, so the check rarely fires for it. (Addendum 11's "Name a primary colour."
miss did not recur at temperature 0 in this harness.)

Whole session with the check on (`docs/benchmark/system_session_escalation.json`):

| Configuration | Session | Median | vs plain | Correct | Peak RAM | Cache / small / 7B | Re-asked |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|---:|
| plain | 428 s | 9.7 s | 1.00x | 34/34 | 5.08 GB | 0 / 0 / 34 | – |
| + 1.5B small model | 275 s | 3.1 s | 1.56x | 34/34 | 6.82 GB | 9 / 14 / 11 | 0 |
| **+ 0.5B small model, shared as draft** | **203 s** | **1.3 s** | **2.11x** | 34/34 | **5.90 GB** | 9 / 12 / 13 | 2 |

Run-to-run spread on this laptop is large (the 1.5B setup measured 2.19x, 1.79x and 1.56x in three
sessions; the shared 0.5B 1.65x and 2.11x), so the two are about equally fast. The shared 0.5B is now
the recommended setup: as accurate or better with the check, and 0.9–1.1 GB less RAM.

## Addendum 14 — drop-in for Ollama and OpenAI clients; memory against Ollama itself, 2026-11-10

`cascade start` runs the model server with `keep_listening`: it answers `/api/chat`, `/api/generate`,
`/api/tags`, `/api/show`, `/api/ps`, `/api/version` (Ollama) and `/v1/chat/completions`, `/v1/models`
(OpenAI), and after `server.idle_minutes` unloads the models instead of exiting. Checked live with the
real Ollama CLI 0.40.15 (`OLLAMA_HOST=127.0.0.1:8765 ollama run qwen2.5-coder ...`) and an OpenAI-style
request, config file containing only `model qwen2.5-coder` (runner, drafting and the shared 0.5B small
model on by default):

| Request | Wall time (client) | Served by |
|---|---:|---|
| `ollama run` "What is the capital of Japan?" | 6.5 s | small model (first request after load) |
| same again | **0.7 s** | cache |
| `ollama run` "Write a Python function that returns the factorial of n." | 23.1 s | 7B, drafting |
| `/v1/chat/completions` "How many legs does a spider have?" | 1.8 s | small model |

Memory, Windows working set (RSS) and committed private bytes:

| Process | Models | RSS | Committed |
|---|---|---:|---:|
| Ollama `llama-server` (num_ctx 2048) | 7B | 5.06 GB | 5.21 GB |
| Cascade server, before this change | 7B + 0.5B + embedder | 5.46 GB | 7.19 GB |
| **Cascade server** | 7B + 0.5B + embedder | **5.47 GB** | **6.61 GB** |
| one llama-cpp-python 7B load, in isolation | 7B | – | 5.43 → **5.14 GB** |

The committed-memory cut: llama-cpp-python allocates a float32 logits buffer per model (here
512 x 152k = 0.29 GB) that neither the windowed speculative eval nor plain decoding writes. It is now
replaced by a one-row buffer at load (verify_greedy still re-creates a full one while it runs);
-0.58 GB for the 7B and the 0.5B. The 7B alone now commits slightly less than Ollama's process, and
the whole Cascade server holds 0.4 GB more working set than Ollama with the 7B alone while also
holding the small model, the embedder and the cache.

## Addendum 15 — a smaller working memory for the 7B, 2026-11-11

On top of the fixed weights, a llama.cpp context holds the KV cache (grows with n_ctx) and a compute
buffer (grows with n_ubatch). `scripts/benchmark_memory_options.py` runs each option in its own process
(400- or 3000-token prompt, 64 greedy tokens) and reports committed private memory, which unlike the
Windows working set is not trimmed by the OS. qwen2.5-coder 7B Q4_K_M, 4-core laptop:

| Option | Committed, n_ctx 2048 | Committed, n_ctx 8192 (3000-token prompt) | Prompt time, 8192 | Same 64 tokens |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| base (f16 KV, n_ubatch 512) | 5.15 GB | 5.74 GB | 221–229 s | – |
| flash attention | – | 5.49 GB | 206 s | yes |
| n_ubatch 256 | 5.00 GB | 5.46 GB | 189 s | yes |
| **flash attention + n_ubatch 256** | **5.00 GB** | **5.34 GB** | 172–191 s | yes |
| + q8_0 KV cache | 4.94 GB | 5.13 GB | 307 s | yes |
| q8_0 K cache only | – | 5.63 GB | 257 s | yes |

Speed on this machine varied a lot between runs today (the same 400-token prompt took 20–30 s), so
every option was repeated; flash attention + n_ubatch 256 was never slower than base. A q8_0 KV cache
saves another 0.2 GB but costs 12–44% prompt speed on this CPU, so it stays off.

Speculative decoding with the new settings, run back to back against the old ones on the same day
(`benchmark_acceleration.py`, confidence drafting p_min 0.75 k 16, greedy lossless check):

| Settings | Decode speed-up | Violations |
|---|---:|---:|
| old | 1.36x | 0 |
| **new** (flash attention + n_ubatch 256) | **1.38x** | 0 |
| old, again | 1.35x | 0 |

(The absolute speed-ups are below earlier days' 1.39–1.61x because the machine was slower overall
today; the comparison is the point.) The runner now loads every model with `flash_attn=True,
n_ubatch=256`: **-0.15 GB at n_ctx 2048, -0.40 GB at 8192** for the 7B, more at longer contexts and for
larger models, with identical output. Results: `docs/benchmark/memory_options_7b_*.json`,
`docs/benchmark/working_memory_ab_*.json`.
